deep.reconstruction:
The page has three parts.

(A) Zeta function, continued from the previous page. There Hilbert proposed, as a route to the theorem on the zeros of zeta, extending zeta(s) to a family zeta(s;x;xi) = sum_n (q-factor)^n cos(nx) cos(n xi) / n^s and writing it as int_0^oo theta(...) t^(...) dt.

The reading that fits the text (my reconstruction) is:
- Take theta(x,t) = sum_n e^{-n^2 t} cos(nx). This is an elliptic theta function, and each term satisfies the heat equation theta_t = theta_xx.
- Since int_0^oo t^{s/2-1} e^{-n^2 t} dt = Gamma(s/2) n^{-s}, one gets Gamma(s/2) sum_n cos(nx) cos(n xi) n^{-s} = int_0^oo t^{s/2-1} sum_n e^{-n^2 t} cos(nx) cos(n xi) dt.
- Using cos(nx)cos(n xi) = (cos n(x+xi) + cos n(x-xi))/2, the kernel is (theta(x+xi,t) + theta(x-xi,t))/2.
- At x = xi = 0 this is Riemann's 1859 theta-integral, i.e. the Mellin transform of theta.

Hilbert's point on this page: zeta appears as int_0^oo of the product of two functions, each satisfying a linear second-order equation. theta satisfies the heat equation (partial). t^{s/2-1} satisfies an ordinary Euler-type equation, e.g. t^2 f'' - (s/2-1)(s/2-2) f = 0. He calls such representations, in his view, a very frequent circumstance in analysis. No further step is taken.

(B) A research question. What are the fundamental solutions of u_xxx + u_y = 0 and of u_xxx + u_yy + u_z = 0? He asks this by analogy with the heat equation u_xx + u_y = 0, whose fundamental solution is found by looking for u depending only on a similarity variable.
- For the heat equation as written the variable is x^2/y. A solution is u = (-y)^{-1/2} exp(x^2/(4y)), i.e. the usual heat kernel with t = -y.
- My completion for u_xxx + u_y = 0: the scaling is x^3 ~ y, so u = y^{-1/3} F(x/y^{1/3}).
  - Substituting gives F''' + (z F)'/3 = 0 with z = x y^{-1/3}.
  - Hence u = (3y)^{-1/3} Ai(x/(3y)^{1/3}). This equals (1/2pi) int e^{i(kx + k^3 y)} dk, the Airy kernel of the linearized KdV equation.
- The mixed equation u_xxx + u_yy + u_z = 0 is only posed; no answer is given.

(C) 'Leftovers from integral equations'. These are remarks on Hilbert's theory of bounded quadratic forms K(x) in infinitely many variables (4th Mitteilung, 1906).

(i) The max/min problem for K on the unit sphere is answered in general by the spectral representation, formerly 'Partialbruchdarstellung'. Point spectrum and continuous ('Strecken-') spectrum together form the spectrum of K.

(ii) A solvability criterion. If the 'Faltung' (composition) of the resolvent form K(lambda; x,.) with itself stays finite as lambda approaches a point nu, then the inhomogeneous equations arising from (x,x) - nu K(x) are always solvable.
- In modern terms: by the resolvent identity, the self-composition of the resolvent is d/d lambda of the resolvent. If it stays bounded, nu is not in the spectrum (or is removable), so I - nu K is invertible.
- He cites Hellinger's Ausarbeitung of Hilbert's 1905/06 course on partial differential equations, pp. 237-240.

(iii) A lemma whose argument finishes on the next page.
- Setup: K is definite with no point spectrum, and K(x) = int_alpha^oo (psi_1(mu)x_1 + psi_2(mu)x_2 + ...)^2 / mu dmu, with alpha the lower end of the continuous spectrum.
- Let lambda_1^(n) be the smallest characteristic value of the section K_n (first n variables). Then 1/lambda_1^(n) = max of K_n on the unit sphere.
- The lambda_1^(n) decrease and accumulate at beta, the point of the spectrum nearest to 0.
- Since K_n(x) = K(x_1..x_n,0,0,...), K attains every value 1/lambda_1^(n) on the unit sphere. Hence values of K come arbitrarily close to 1/beta.
- Completeness gives (x,x) = int_alpha^oo (sum psi_p x_p)^2 dmu. So K(x) <= (1/alpha)(x,x), giving 1/beta <= 1/alpha, i.e. beta >= alpha.
- Conversely, alpha lies in the spectrum and beta is the nearest spectral point to 0, so beta <= alpha. Therefore alpha = beta.
- This is the infinite-dimensional Rayleigh principle: sup of K on the unit sphere = 1/(bottom of the spectrum), approximated by the finite sections.
errors: Heat-equation analogy: the transcription reads 'u depending only on y^2/x'. For u_xx + u_y = 0 the similarity variable is x^2/y (or y/x^2). y^2/x is a slip of the pen or a misreading; either way it cannot be right as written.

The lemma says 'die lambda=0 naechstgelegene Stelle des Punktspektrums sei beta', yet K is assumed to have no point spectrum. The intended meaning is the nearest point of the spectrum, i.e. the accumulation point of the section eigenvalues. This is a verbal slip.

On the next page Hilbert concludes from 1/beta <= 1/alpha 'd.h. alpha >= beta'. The correct consequence (both positive) is alpha <= beta. The second argument then gives beta <= alpha. So the conclusion alpha = beta is right, but one inequality is stated in the wrong direction.

Unjustified step: 'values of K come arbitrarily close to 1/beta' needs lambda_1^(n) -> beta. This holds because the maxima of the sections increase monotonically to the supremum of K on the unit sphere. Hilbert asserts it ('gewiss') without proof.

The zeta sketch (via the previous page) gives no argument toward the zeros. It is only a heuristic remark about Mellin-type product representations. The factor 'y^n' in the series is unclear and is presumably a theta-type factor such as e^{-n^2 t}.

results.what: zeta(s) (generalized by cos nx cos n xi) as int_0^oo theta(x,t) t^{s/2-1} dt, with theta solving the heat equation; viewed as an integral of a product of two solutions of second-order linear equations
results.modern_name: Riemann's theta-integral / Mellin transform of the Jacobi theta function

results.what: Question of fundamental (similarity) solutions of u_xxx + u_y = 0 and u_xxx + u_yy + u_z = 0, by analogy with the heat kernel
results.modern_name: Airy-function fundamental solution of the linearized KdV equation; self-similar solutions
results.usually_credited_to: Airy integrals (Airy 1838, Stokes); third-order 'heat equation' kernels studied e.g. by Bernstein, Block (c. 1910s) and later

results.what: Extremal values of an infinite quadratic form via the spectral representation; point plus continuous spectrum
results.modern_name: Spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint forms; Rayleigh/min-max principle

results.what: Boundedness of the self-composition of the resolvent near nu implies solvability of the inhomogeneous equations for (x,x) - nu K(x)
results.modern_name: Resolvent criterion: d/dlambda R(lambda) = R(lambda)^2 bounded near nu means nu is in the resolvent set

results.what: For definite K with only continuous spectrum starting at alpha, the smallest eigenvalues of the finite sections converge to alpha
results.modern_name: Convergence of Rayleigh-Ritz / section approximations to the bottom of the spectrum

deep.surprise_reason: The spectral-theory material is Hilbert's own published 1906 theory and is routine. The zeta remark is Riemann's theta-Mellin integral plus a philosophical comment, though it documents Hilbert privately looking for an analytic route to the zeros of zeta, which has mild historical interest given the Hilbert-Polya lore. The Airy-type fundamental solution is only asked as a question.

transcription_corrections: 'K(x)' throughout should be the Fraktur form (as on the next page's transcription), denoting the quadratic form.
'(x'x) - nu K(x)' should read '(x,x) - nu K(x)', the unit form minus nu times K.
In 'nur von y^2/x abhängen' the intended similarity variable for the heat equation is x^2/y. The manuscript may in fact read so, or it is Hilbert's slip.
'Faltung von K(lambda; a, ...) K(lambda; a.)' is more plausibly 'K(lambda; x, .) K(lambda; x, .)', the composition of the resolvent form with itself.
'Hellinger Ausarbeitung [-...-] Kolleg' presumably refers to Hellinger's Ausarbeitung of Hilbert's Kolleg on partial differential equations, 1905/06.
'also [-sich-] stellt sich' should read 'also stellt sich' (the first 'sich' is struck out).
